column1: What is the primary difference between Angular and a library like React regarding built-in tooling?
column2:
Angular is a full, opinionated platform that includes built-in solutions for routing, forms, HTTP client, and CLI out of the box.

React is a UI rendering library where developers assemble third-party libraries for routing, state management, and HTTP.

column1: How does declarative data binding in Angular differ from imperative DOM manipulation in plain JavaScript?
column2:
Imperative (Vanilla JS): You manually write step-by-step instructions to locate and update DOM elements (e.g. document.getElementById().textContent = ...).

Declarative (Angular): You declare the UI relationship once in the template, and Angular automatically updates the DOM when underlying class data changes.

column1: What is the main architectural difference between AngularJS (1.x) and modern Angular (2+)?
column2:
AngularJS (1.x): Based on Controllers, $scope, and JavaScript.

Modern Angular (2+): Based on a Component-Tree architecture (Class + Template + Scoped Styles), TypeScript, and an improved change detection model.

column1: What does the CLI command ng serve do?
column2: It builds the application, starts a local development server (default http://localhost:4200), and watches project files to automatically rebuild and live-reload the browser when changes are saved.

column1: What Angular CLI command generates a new component named dessert-card?
column2:
ng generate component dessert-card
(or shortcut: ng g component dessert-card)

column1: In modern standalone Angular, how do you make a child component DessertCard usable inside a parent component's template?
column2: Import the DessertCard class directly into the imports: [...] array of the parent component's @Component decorator.

column1: What role does src/index.html play in an Angular application?
column2: It is the single real HTML page loaded by the browser. Angular dynamically mounts and renders the root component (e.g., <app-root></app-root>) inside this file.

column1: What is the difference in scope between src/styles.css and a component's dessert-card.css file?
column2:
src/styles.css: Defines global styles that apply across the entire application.

dessert-card.css: Styles are scoped exclusively to DessertCard via Angular's default View Encapsulation.

column1: What three main building blocks make up an Angular component?
column2:
1. TypeScript Class: Contains properties (data) and methods (logic).
2. HTML Template: Defines the view using Angular template syntax.
3. CSS Styles: Defines scoped styling for the component.

column1: What is the purpose of the selector property in the @Component decorator?
column2: It specifies the custom HTML tag name (e.g., selector: 'app-dessert-card') used in templates to instantiate and render that component (e.g., <app-dessert-card></app-dessert-card>).

column1: List the four main types of data binding in Angular and their syntaxes.
column2:
1. Interpolation: {{ value }} (Class → Template text)
2. Property Binding: [property]="value" (Class → Template DOM property)
3. Event Binding: (event)="handler()" (Template → Class)
4. Two-Way Binding: [(ngModel)]="value" (Class ↔ Template)

column1: Why does <button disabled="{{ isAvailable }}"> fail to disable/enable a button as expected?
column2:
Interpolation converts values to strings. In HTML, the mere presence of the disabled attribute (even as "false") disables the button.

Solution: Use Property Binding [disabled]="!isAvailable" to pass the raw boolean value to the DOM property.

column1: What types of operations should NOT be placed inside template interpolation {{ }}?
column2:
Assignments (e.g. x = 5), side-effects, new expressions, or multi-statement logic.

Interpolation expects a single expression that evaluates to a displayable value.

column1: What is the purpose of the special $event variable in event binding (input)="onInput($event)"?
column2: $event passes the native DOM event object (or custom emitted payload) into the component method, allowing access to event details like (event.target as HTMLInputElement).value.

column1: What is the syntax for two-way data binding in Angular, and what is its popular visual mnemonic?
column2:
Syntax: [(ngModel)]="property"

Mnemonic: "Banana in a box" (parentheses () inside square brackets []).

column1: Which module must be imported for [(ngModel)] to work in Angular templates?
column2: FormsModule (imported from @angular/forms).

column1: What two bindings does [(ngModel)]="dessertName" expand to under the hood?
column2:
It combines property binding and custom event binding:
[ngModel]="dessertName" (ngModelChange)="dessertName = $event"

column1: What is the core difference between a Structural Directive and an Attribute Directive?
column2:
Structural Directives (prefixed with *): Add or remove elements directly from the DOM (e.g., *ngIf, *ngFor).

Attribute Directives (use []): Modify the appearance or behavior of an existing DOM element without altering DOM structure (e.g., [ngClass], [ngStyle]).

column1: What actually happens to an element in the DOM when *ngIf="false" evaluates to false?
column2:
Angular completely destroys and removes the element (and its child components) from the DOM.

(Unlike CSS display: none, which leaves the element in the DOM tree).

column1: How do you write an *ngIf directive with an else fallback template?
column2:
<p *ngIf="desserts.length > 0; else noDesserts">Available!</p>
<ng-template #noDesserts>
<p>No desserts available.</p>
</ng-template>

column1: Why can't you place both *ngIf and *ngFor directly on the exact same HTML element?
column2:
Angular prohibits multiple structural directives on a single element due to ambiguity in execution order.

Solution: Wrap one directive in an <ng-container> block.

column1: In *ngFor="let dessert of desserts; let i = index", what does let i = index provide?
column2: It exposes the current zero-based array index of the iteration as a local template variable named i.

column1: What is the purpose of trackBy in an *ngFor list iteration?
column2: It provides Angular with a unique identifier (e.g., dessert.id) to track items. This allows Angular to reuse existing DOM elements when array references update, avoiding expensive full re-renders.

column1: What is the syntax for ngClass when toggling multiple classes based on conditions?
column2: [ngClass]="{ 'sold-out': !dessert.available, 'featured': dessert.isFeatured }"

column1: When should you prefer [class.sold-out]="condition" over [ngClass]?
column2: When you only need to toggle a single CSS class based on a single condition. It is cleaner and simpler than defining an object in ngClass.

column1: How does a parent component pass data down to a child component?
column2:
1. In child class: Decorate property with @Input() (e.g., @Input() dessert!: Dessert;).
2. In parent template: Use property binding (e.g., <app-dessert-card [dessert]="selectedDessert"></app-dessert-card>).

column1: How does a child component emit events up to a parent component?
column2:
1. In child class: Define @Output() selected = new EventEmitter<Dessert>(); and call this.selected.emit(dessertPayload);.
2. In parent template: Listen using event binding (selected)="onDessertSelected($event)".

column1: In a parent listening to a child's custom event (selected)="handleSelection($event)", what is $event?
column2: $event is the exact payload data passed into the child's this.selected.emit(payload) call.

column1: Why should initialization logic that depends on @Input() properties be placed in ngOnInit() instead of the class constructor()?
column2: During constructor() execution, Angular has not yet initialized @Input() properties (they will be undefined). ngOnInit() runs after Angular sets all input properties.

column1: What does the non-null assertion operator ! mean in @Input() dessert!: Dessert;?
column2: It informs the TypeScript compiler that dessert will be initialized by Angular before it is accessed, suppressing strict property initialization error checks.
